anchor: Shut, shut the door, good John!
title: Title, occasion and form
short: A verse letter (published January 1735) to Pope's friend and physician John Arbuthnot, then dying, in which Pope defends his life and his satire.
body: John Arbuthnot (1667-1735), Scottish physician to Queen Anne, wit and fellow Scriblerian, wrote to Pope in July 1734 from what he knew was his deathbed, urging him to continue his 'disdain and abhorrence of vice' but with prudence; Pope replied that general satire was useless without examples. The poem, dated 1734 and issued on 2 January 1735, was assembled from earlier fragments in answer to attacks by 'persons of rank and fortune', the Verses to the Imitator of Horace (1733) by Lady Mary Wortley Montagu and Lord Hervey, and Hervey's Epistle to a Doctor of Divinity. It opens in the middle of a domestic scene: 'good John' is Pope's servant John Serle. In later editions it became the 'Prologue to the Satires', and the text is set out as a dialogue between P. and A. after Horace's Satires 2.1. Arbuthnot died in February 1735.

title: The Dog-star rages!
short: Sirius, rising in late summer, was believed to bring heat, fever and madness; the season of 'dog days' is also the season of bad poets reciting.
body: The heliacal rising of Sirius in July and August was associated with heat, plague and madness. Juvenal complains of poets reciting in August (Satire 3.9), and Horace pictures the mad poet as a plague to be fled (Ars Poetica 453-76). 'Bedlam' (Bethlehem Hospital, London's madhouse) and 'Parnassus' (the Muses' mountain) are equated: the hospital's inmates and the poets have broken loose together, with 'fire' in their eyes and manuscripts in their hands.

title: the Mint; Twit'nam
short: The Mint in Southwark was a sanctuary where debtors could not be arrested; on Sundays they could walk abroad freely, so the Sabbath brings Pope no rest.
body: Debtors could not be arrested on Sundays, so the Sunday release of impoverished poets from their refuge in the Southwark Mint makes even the Sabbath unsafe. Pope's villa at Twickenham ('Twit'nam', the local pronunciation), leased from 1719, with its garden 'thickets' and the famous grotto under the road, is besieged by land and water: poets stop his chariot and board his barge on the Thames. The comedy of persecution introduces the theme of the poem: Pope as the reluctant victim of other people's bad verse.

title: engross
short: A lawyer's clerk who writes verse when he should be engrossing, that is, copying documents out fair in legal hand.
body: To 'engross' (OED) is to write out a legal document in large, formal script; the clerk is 'foredoom'd' to disappoint his father, who sent him to the law. The catalogue of would-be poets (drunken parson, maudlin poetess, rhyming peer, clerk, madman scrawling with charcoal on his cell wall) gives a social panorama of the scribbling mania. 'Arthur' is Arthur Moore, whose son James Moore Smythe had used Pope's verses in his comedy The Rival Modes; 'Cornus' (Latin cornu, horn) marks a cuckold whose wife has eloped.

title: Friend to my life!
short: Pope turns to Arbuthnot as the doctor who has preserved his life, and wryly blames him for the 'idle songs' that life has produced.
body: Pope suffered from tuberculosis of the spine (Pott's disease), which left him about four and a half feet tall and frequently ill; Arbuthnot attended him. The medical vocabulary ('drop', 'nostrum', 'plague') runs through the poem and returns in 'this long disease, my life'. The 'dire dilemma' is comic: whether foes write against him or friends read their works to him, he is 'read dead'.

title: Keep your piece nine years
short: Horace's advice to poets (Ars Poetica 388): keep a work back until the ninth year, revising before publishing.
body: Horace tells the Pisos to lock a manuscript away 'nonumque prematur in annum', until the ninth year, because what is unpublished can still be destroyed and what is published cannot be recalled. The hack poet who lives 'high in Drury-lane' (in a garret, near the theatres and brothels) cannot wait: he writes in bed, publishes before the end of the law 'Term' (the booksellers' season) and blames hunger and the 'request of friends', a stock excuse in prefaces.

title: Pitholeon; Curll; Lintot
short: Pitholeon, a bad poet in Horace, stands for a libeller now seeking favours; Edmund Curll and Bernard Lintot were booksellers with whom Pope had long dealings.
body: Horace mentions Pitholeon of Rhodes as a poet who mixed Greek and Latin (Satires 1.10.22); Lynch notes Pope's own gloss on the name. The modern Pitholeon wants Pope to recommend him to a duke despite having libelled him. Edmund Curll, the notorious publisher of piracies and scandal, had printed Pope's letters without leave; he will employ the man to write a journal or turn divine. Lintot, Pope's own publisher for the Iliad, is 'dull rogue'. The scene ends in the slang proposal 'we go snacks' (share the profits), and Pope slams the door.

title: Midas' ears
short: Midas, given ass's ears by Apollo; his secret was betrayed by a servant, or in another version his queen. In Pope's version the minister (some say the queen) is forced to speak; contemporaries could read a hint at the court.
body: In Ovid (Metamorphoses 11.172-93) Apollo punishes Midas for preferring Pan's music by giving him ass's ears; his barber, unable to keep the secret, whispered it into a hole in the ground, and reeds sang it abroad. In Chaucer's Wife of Bath's Tale the teller is Midas's wife. Persius (Satire 1.121) asked who has not the ears of an ass, a line said originally to have named Midas the king. Pope's 'minister' and 'queen' (the one who first spied the ears must speak or burst, 'some say his queen') could be read as pointing dangerously at Walpole and Queen Caroline, which is why Arbuthnot warns him off naming 'queens, ministers, or kings'.

title: The dialogue form
short: Arbuthnot's cautious interruptions recall Horace Satires 2.1, where the lawyer Trebatius warns the satirist of danger; the half-lines create real conversation.
body: Pope had imitated Horace's Satires 2.1 in 1733, a dialogue with a prudent legal adviser. In this poem the friend's warnings ('No names', 'learn prudence of a friend') allow Pope to justify the naming of names. Several speeches break off mid-line ('Still Sappho----', 'Let Sporus tremble--') and are completed by the other speaker, so that the heroic couplet is broken and reassembled in dialogue. Speaker labels are a feature of the later, revised text.

title: the scribbler's cobweb
short: The bad writer is a spider spinning flimsy lines from himself; brush the web away and he spins it again.
body: The image of the spider spinning from its own entrails had been used by Swift in The Battle of the Books (1704) for modern authors who draw everything from themselves, against the bee who gathers from nature and the ancients. Pope extends it into a mock-heroic picture of the scribbler enthroned 'in the centre of his thin designs', proud of 'a vast extent of flimsy lines'. 'Codrus' is a conventional name for a bad poet from Juvenal (Satire 1.2), who cannot be shamed, and the 'bursting world' echoes Horace's just man unshaken by a falling universe (Odes 3.3.7-8).

title: Colly; Henley; Moore; Bavius; Philips; Sappho
short: A roll-call of enemies: Colley Cibber, 'Orator' John Henley, James Moore Smythe, Bavius (a bad poet in Virgil), Ambrose Philips, and 'Sappho', Lady Mary Wortley Montagu.
body: Colley Cibber, actor-manager and Poet Laureate from 1730, later the king of the revised Dunciad, has his lord and mistress; John Henley, a preacher who lectured to butchers in his 'Oratory', has his audience; Moore Smythe, his freemasons. Bavius is the poetaster of Virgil, Eclogue 3.90. Ambrose Philips, Pope's old pastoral rival, was secretary to Archbishop Boulter in Ireland, the 'bishop' who thought him a wit. 'Sappho' was Pope's name for Lady Mary, his former friend and co-author of the attack of 1733; the friend stops Pope before he names her.

title: Ammon's great son; Ovid's nose; Maro
short: Flatterers compare Pope's physical defects to those of the great: Horace's cough, Alexander's high shoulder, Ovid's nose, Virgil's drooping head.
body: Alexander the Great, saluted as son of the god Ammon, was said to carry his head or one shoulder awry; Ovid's cognomen Naso means 'nose'; Horace mentions his own short stature and ill health, and Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro) was said to be sickly. Pope, a hunchback barely four and a half feet tall, sees through the compliment: such flattery makes him a museum of other men's deformities. The punch line, that Homer died three thousand years ago, mocks hyperbolic comparisons with ancient genius.

title: I lisp'd in numbers; this long disease, my life
short: Pope's autobiography of his vocation: he wrote verse as a child, as Ovid did, and poetry consoled a life of illness.
body: 'I lisp'd in numbers, for the numbers came' recalls Ovid's autobiographical elegy (Tristia 4.10.25-26), where whatever he tried to say came out as verse. 'Numbers' are metrical lines. Pope stresses that poetry broke no duty: his Catholic family barred him from the universities, public office and many professions, so 'I left no calling'. The phrase 'this long disease, my life' turns his chronic illness into an emblem of mortal existence; the Muse helped him 'to bear' the life Arbuthnot preserved.

title: Granville, Walsh, Garth, Congreve, Swift ... St John
short: The great patrons and wits who encouraged the young Pope, among them Dryden's own friends.
body: George Granville, Lord Lansdowne, and William Walsh, the critic who told Pope to aim at 'correctness', praised his Pastorals; Sir Samuel Garth, physician-poet, Congreve and Swift were friends; Charles Talbot, Duke of Shrewsbury, Lord Somers and John Sheffield, Duke of Buckingham, read his work; 'mitred Rochester' is Francis Atterbury, Bishop of Rochester; St John is Henry St John, Viscount Bolingbroke. The roll of approving great men is set against the hacks Burnet, Oldmixon and Cooke, who had attacked him. Pope's own note says these men had all been patrons or admirers of Dryden (the line calls them 'great Dryden's friends before'), and he had seen Dryden as a boy at Will's coffee-house.

title: in amber ... hairs, or straws, or dirt, or grubs, or worms
short: Pedantic editors, preserved by the great authors they annotate, are like insects and straws caught in amber.
body: 'Slashing Bentley' is Richard Bentley, the great classical scholar, whose edition of Paradise Lost (1732) emended or cut hundreds of lines; 'piddling Tibbalds' is Lewis Theobald, who exposed errors in Pope's Shakespeare in Shakespeare Restored (1726) and became the hero of the first Dunciad. The amber conceit goes back to Martial's epigrams on a bee, a viper and an ant preserved in amber (4.32, 4.59, 6.15). The list of worthless contents mimics the editors' fussy attention to trivia, and the closing couplet wonders 'how the devil' they got into such company.

title: Atticus
short: The famous portrait of Joseph Addison, an ideal man of letters spoiled by jealousy, who rules a literary coterie and damns rivals with faint praise.
body: Addison (1672-1719), essayist of The Spectator and author of the tragedy Cato (1713), for which Pope wrote the prologue, presided at Button's coffee-house over a group of Whig writers ('his little senate'). Pope believed Addison had encouraged Thomas Tickell's rival translation of the Iliad (1715). The lines were drafted soon after and circulated and printed in various forms from the 1720s, long after Addison's death, which some readers thought ungenerous; Johnson notes that the closing couplet was twice corrected before it reached its final form. Like an Ottoman sultan who kills his brothers on accession, he bears 'no brother near the throne'. The name recalls Cicero's friend Titus Pomponius Atticus, a model of urbane detachment. The portrait's balance ('willing to wound, and yet afraid to strike') makes the antithetical couplet itself an image of hesitation.

title: Bufo
short: Bufo (Latin 'toad') is a composite portrait of the vain literary patron, sometimes identified with Charles Montagu, Lord Halifax, and George Bubb Dodington.
body: Bufo sits 'proud as Apollo on his forked hill' (Parnassus, with two peaks), fed with dedications, his library adorned with busts of dead poets, including a headless 'true Pindar'. He pays poets in port, praise or a reading of his own verse. 'Castalian state' is the realm of poetry, after the Castalian spring on Parnassus. The bitterest couplet concerns Dryden, who died in 1700 in neglect after losing his offices at the Revolution and was then buried with ceremony in Westminster Abbey: 'He help'd to bury whom he help'd to starve.'

title: Gay; Queensberry
short: John Gay, poet of The Beggar's Opera and Pope's close friend, died in December 1732 after years of disappointed hopes of court patronage.
body: Pope ironically thanks the great for leaving him Gay, whom they neglected. Gay (1685-1732) had been offered only a minor post as gentleman usher to a young princess, which he refused; in his last years he lived with the Duke and Duchess of Queensberry, who put up his monument in Westminster Abbey with Pope's epitaph. The couplet's pathos ('My verse, and Queensberry weeping o'er thy urn!') is one of the poem's tonal shifts from satire to elegy.

title: Sporus
short: Sporus, the boy Nero castrated and married, is Pope's name for Lord Hervey, vice-chamberlain and confidant of Queen Caroline, co-author of the 1733 attack on Pope.
body: Suetonius (Nero 28) tells how Nero had the boy Sporus castrated and went through a form of marriage with him. John, Lord Hervey (1696-1743), was a brilliant, sickly courtier who wore cosmetics and lived on a diet that included ass's milk, hence 'white curd of ass's milk'; Pope had already called him 'Lord Fanny' (compare 'gentle Fanny' earlier in this poem). The name insinuates effeminacy and sexual ambiguity, as Lynch notes. Arbuthnot's protest, 'Who breaks a butterfly upon a wheel?', alludes to breaking on the wheel, a form of execution: too severe for so slight a creature. Pope's answer turns the butterfly into a gilded bug that 'stinks and stings'. The portrait's ferocity has been both admired as the summit of English satire and condemned as personal cruelty.

title: at the ear of Eve
short: Milton's Satan crouches 'squat like a toad' at Eve's ear; Hervey whispers to Queen Caroline in the same posture.
body: In Paradise Lost IV.799-800 Satan is found 'squat like a toad, close at the ear of Eve', breathing dreams into her mind. Hervey's place at court gave him the queen's ear, and Pope casts him as the tempter. 'Familiar' means both intimate and a witch's familiar spirit. The portrait culminates in another Satanic image, the tempter as described by rabbinic commentators, with a cherub's face on a reptile's body: 'Wit that can creep, and pride that licks the dust' recalls the curse on the serpent (Genesis 3:14).

title: one vile antithesis; Amphibious thing
short: Pope makes Sporus embody the figure of antithesis: he is 'all see-saw', both sexes, both parts, a living contradiction.
body: The lines on Sporus pile up balanced oppositions ('now high, now low', 'trifling head, or the corrupted heart', 'Fop at the toilet, flatterer at the board', 'trips a lady, and now struts a lord'). Antithesis is the essential figure of the Augustan couplet, and Pope reflexively turns his own technique into an image of moral corruption: Hervey is 'one vile antithesis'. 'Amphibious' (living a double life) completes the bestiary of bug, spaniel, puppet and toad.

title: stoop'd to Truth, and moralised his song
short: A falconry metaphor: a hawk 'stoops' when it swoops on its prey; Pope descended from fanciful description to moral truth.
body: The phrase marks the turn in Pope's career from the descriptive and imaginative poetry of his youth (the Pastorals, Windsor-Forest, The Rape of the Lock) to the ethical poetry of An Essay on Man and the Moral Essays. 'Stoop' in falconry is the sudden descent of a hawk on its quarry (OED), so humility and energetic attack are combined. The passage is Pope's self-portrait as the satirist who endures abuse for virtue's sake.

title: Welsted; Budgell; the two Curlls
short: Leonard Welsted, Eustace Budgell, and the 'two Curlls' (the bookseller and Lord Hervey) as slanderers whom Pope long left unanswered.
body: Pope's note says Welsted had printed that Pope caused a lady's death and had libelled the Duke of Chandos, from whom Welsted claimed to have received £500, and that the Duke knew both charges false; 'three thousand suns' (about eight years) went down on the lie. Budgell abused Pope in his paper The Bee over a piece in which Pope had no hand; he was also suspected of forging the will of Matthew Tindal (1733) in his own favour, hence 'except his will'. The 'two Curlls of town and court' are Edmund Curll and Hervey, who had attacked Pope's father and his deformity.

title: Pope's parents
short: Pope's portrait of his father, a retired Catholic linen merchant who died in 1717, and of his mother Edith, who died in June 1733.
body: Hervey and Lady Mary had sneered at Pope's low birth. Pope claims gentle descent for both parents (his note mentions relatives killed for the king in the Civil War) and contrasts their honest fortune with 'Bestia's from the throne', Lucius Calpurnius Bestia, the Roman consul bribed by Jugurtha (Sallust), probably glancing at the Duke of Marlborough. His father, 'stranger to civil and religious rage', was a Catholic who withdrew from London under the penal laws. 'Innoxious' means harmless. The lines on tending 'a mother's breath' were written while Edith Pope lived but published after her death, an affecting discrepancy noted by editors.

title: Closing prayer and Arbuthnot's reply
short: Pope prays for Arbuthnot as he prays to nurse his mother; the doctor's last line commits the rest to Heaven.
body: Arbuthnot had been physician to Queen Anne and lost his court place at her death in 1714; Pope wishes him 'just as rich' as he was then, a compliment to his integrity. The final couplet, spoken by Arbuthnot, restores the epistle's frame of friendship and piety. Arbuthnot died on 27 February 1735, a few weeks after the poem was published, which gives the ending an added poignancy for later readers.
